ch09.card: Part 8 of 10. Does the thinking really do the work?
ch09.s01.c1: Bold claim: the thinking does the work. Let us try to break it. The thinker is a team of note-takers, and one lap is one round.
ch09.s01.c2: This chapter tests that claim, on an older design with 12 fixed rounds and a calculator built in.
ch09.s02.c1: Our model scored 73.01 points out of 100 on 6,040 questions kept aside.
ch09.s02.c2: That is 4,410 right. Is that good? Alone, you cannot tell. So: is it the thinking that earns them?
ch09.s03.c1: Our exam is 6,040 questions kept aside. None were used in practice. A fair test.
ch09.s03.c2: Five kinds, from familiar to brand new.
ch09.s03.c3: They add up to 6,040. The test is called pooled-5: mixed into a single score.
ch09.s04.c1: Now the fun part. Trained with 12 rounds, it scores 73.01 at 12.
ch09.s04.c2: I turn the thinking dial down, no new practice. At 2 rounds, it scores 29.30.
ch09.s04.c4: And now none. 0 rounds, no thinking at all: 0.66. Just 40 right out of 6,040.
ch09.s05.c1: More thinking must help more, right? Turn the dial past its practice, to 24 rounds.
ch09.s05.c2: The score does not rise. It is 72.57, which is 27 fewer right: 4,410 minus 4,383.
ch09.s05.c3: The design we plan to ship adds a learned stop switch, a bell that picks the number of rounds. Built, but never tested.
ch09.s06.c1: A second test, called chain-5: 1,000 multi-step questions kept aside. Several sums in a row.
ch09.s06.c2: Each calculator step takes its own round, so cutting rounds should hurt most. What would you guess?
ch09.s07.c1: Now we break things on purpose. A lesion test: break one part, and see if the answer breaks.
ch09.s07.c2: Hand the talker, which writes the answer, another question's notes. The score falls to 4.19 on familiar questions.
ch09.s07.c3: Shuffle the notes between questions: 6.80. A wiring check. It shows plumbing, not good reasoning.
ch09.s08.c1: Now a sneaky trick. Swap add and subtract in the calculator, plain code that does the sums.
ch09.s08.c2: Will the model notice? Of 831 answers the swap changes, 830 followed it.
ch09.s08.c3: Switch it off: 0.0 on 2,085 questions that need it.
ch09.s09.c1: Now, a mystery. At zero rounds a model should score near zero. Some runs did not. A leak.
ch09.s09.c2: An earlier version, copy 200, scored 18.09 with the borrowed Gemma reader, and 1.40 without it. Its other copy, 201: 4.49 and 4.34.
ch09.s09.c3: Our copy 400: 0.96 here, 0.66 on all 6,040. And why? The cause is not settled.
ch09.s10.c1: Now, side by side with a plain model. On this one copy, ours scores 5.9 points more: 73.01 minus 67.12.
ch09.s10.c2: But here is the twist. It took 2.7 times longer to train in this run: 6.51 hours by 2.38.
ch09.s10.c3: Add a calculator to the plain model, no retraining: 69.62 and 99.0. The gap shrinks to 3.39 points.
ch09.s11.c1: Before you get excited. As of Oct 9, one copy at the smallest size is a first result, not proof.
ch09.s11.c2: This is the older design, 12 fixed rounds, calculator built in. It says nothing yet about bigger sizes.
ch09.s12.c1: Three things to remember. Less thinking, lower score: 73.01 to 0.66. Multi-step answers fall hardest: 99.9 to 0.0 at one round. One copy, smallest size, as of Oct 9: first result, not proof. Next: learning while it sleeps, and a creative mode for when it gets stuck.
